label: Fatigue
title: Tired driving
headline: You can't fight sleep at the wheel
intro: Namibia's long, straight roads make tired driving easy and deadly. See how far you travel in a microsleep, and plan a safer trip.

topics.title: Microsleeps
topics.blurb: A few seconds with your eyes shut

scenes.question: A microsleep is a brief sleep you don't control. Up to how many seconds can it last?

lines: You left Windhoek after work and you're heading north on the B1. It's dark and the road is straight.
Your eyes feel heavy, but you only have a couple of hours to go.

art.alt: A straight tarred road at night, lit only by headlights.

scenes.prompt: At {n:120} km/h, see how far the car travels while your eyes are shut.

art.alt: Night on the road. The screen goes dark while the car keeps moving and drifts toward the edge.

states.label: {n:1} second
states.caption: In just {n:1} second you travel {var:distM} m with nobody steering.

states.label: {n:3} seconds
states.caption: {n:3} seconds: {var:distM} m, enough to drift right off the road.

states.label: {n:5} seconds
states.caption: {n:5} seconds: {var:distM} m. You won't remember it happened.

scenes.explain: A microsleep can last up to {claim:int.fatigue.microsleep}. After {claim:int.fatigue.awake} awake, people perform as badly as, or worse than, someone over the alcohol limit.

questions.prompt: Which are signs that you're too tired to drive? Pick all that apply.
questions.reason: All of these are warning signs. By the time you notice them, a microsleep could be close.
Only sleep fixes tiredness. Fresh air and music don't keep you awake for long.

lines: If you're tired, stop. Only sleep fixes tiredness.
Don't drive late at night after a full day's work.
Share the driving on long trips.

scenes.question: On a long trip, how often should you take a break, at least?

scenes.prompt: You're driving from Windhoek to Oshakati, about {claim:na.stat.b1-distance}. You've been driving for two hours. Where will you stop for a break?

art.alt: A schematic map of the B1 north from Windhoek, with towns, a lay-by and a fuel stop.

points.label: Otjiwarongo
points.title: A good break
points.reason: After about two hours, stop in a town: get out, stretch, eat, and swap drivers if you can. Take at least {claim:int.uk.break}.

points.label: Push on to Tsumeb
points.title: Too long without a break
points.reason: Pushing on adds more hours at the wheel. Tiredness builds without you noticing.

points.label: Keep going to Oshakati
points.title: Don't drive it in one go
points.reason: Driving the whole way without a break is how microsleeps happen.

scenes.explain: Take a break at least every {claim:int.uk.break-every}, for at least {claim:int.uk.break}. For some heavy and passenger vehicles, a planned Namibian rule would limit driving to {claim:na.law.driving-hours} without a break.

lines: Plan your breaks before you set off: at least every two hours.
Start the trip rested, and drive in daylight when you can.
If you feel sleepy, stop somewhere safe and nap.

scenes.title: Nearly home
scenes.label: A made-up story, based on common situations
scenes.warning: This story mentions a crash. Nobody's injuries are described in detail.
paragraphs: Maria had worked a full shift before driving north to see her family. She'd done the trip many times.
Past Tsumeb her eyes kept closing. She opened the window and turned the radio up.
The next thing she remembers is the car bouncing over the gravel shoulder. She stopped just short of a fence post.
'I was lucky,' she says. 'Now I sleep first and leave in the morning.'

signpost.text: If a crash has affected you or someone close to you, you don't have to deal with it alone. LifeLine/ChildLine Namibia offers free counselling: call {claim:na.support.lifeline}.
